# 01 Overview {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## Recommendations Everywhere

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Everyday surfaces**

Video, music, shopping, news, jobs, dating, maps, social feeds, and course resources.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Inputs** — behaviour, context, item attributes, social signals<br>
**Outputs** — a shortlist, ranking, or exposure decision
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
A recommender does not merely retrieve information. It helps decide what receives attention — and what remains unseen.
:::

::: notes
Ask students to name one recommendation they acted on in the last 24 hours. Use the answers to establish that recommendation is a general pattern, not a feature of only one platform.
:::

## Video Sampler

Play **one** short excerpt in class; keep the others as backups. These are external links and require a network connection.

- **Default:** [How Spotify’s AI-Driven Recommendations Work — WSJ Tech Behind](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pGntmcy_HX8), 0:00–2:59 — personalised playlists, user data, and content signals.
- **Technical backup:** [The Math Behind Recommender Systems — Art of the Problem](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n3RKsY2H-NE), 0:00–4:36 — content filtering versus collaborative filtering.

::: notes
Use the WSJ excerpt as the default choice. Pause once and ask students which signals they heard. Verify video availability and classroom playback before delivery.
:::

## AI Voice Mode

Ask the voice-mode agent:

> Give one ordinary example of a recommendation a student might encounter today. Identify the user signal, item, likely objective, and one possible social or ethical consequence. Keep the answer under 45 seconds.

Students compare the agent’s example with their own activity responses. Treat the agent as a conversation partner, not an authority.

::: notes
Start the voice-mode interaction and stop it after two minutes. Correct any claim that treats the agent’s example as a definitive description of a platform’s production system.
:::

## Ethics Thread

- Recommendation systems allocate **attention, visibility, and opportunity**.
- Historical data and engagement objectives can reproduce or amplify **bias**.
- Personalisation raises questions about **privacy, transparency, exposure, fairness, and stakeholder impact**.

::: notes
Frame ethics as a recurring motif rather than a standalone final topic. Ask students to listen for the same questions whenever a later lecture introduces a new model or metric. Keep the optional recommendation-algorithm video in the instructor’s delivery notes as a backup.
:::

# 04 Types of Recommendation Systems {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## A Card-Suit Framework for User Types

We can think about different **user archetypes** using a card-suit analogy:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
♠ **Spades — The Explorer**
- Seeks novelty and diversity
- Values serendipitous discovery
- Dislikes filter bubbles

♥ **Hearts — The Social Connector**
- Influenced by friends and community
- Trusts collaborative signals
- Values shared tastes
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
♦ **Diamonds — The Pragmatist**
- Goal-oriented, task-driven
- Wants the most relevant result fast
- Values precision over diversity

♣ **Clubs — The Loyalist**
- Sticks to known preferences
- Values consistency and familiarity
- Resistant to change
:::
:::

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): How did Min introduce this framework? Was it from a specific paper or his own framing? Were there other user types discussed? -->
:::

## Matching Systems to User Types

Different recommendation paradigms serve different user archetypes:

| User Type | Best-Suited Approach | Key Objective |
|-----------|---------------------|---------------|
| ♠ Explorer | Diversity-aware / serendipity models | Novelty, coverage |
| ♥ Social Connector | Collaborative filtering, social graphs | Community similarity |
| ♦ Pragmatist | Retrieval-ranking pipelines | Precision, relevance |
| ♣ Loyalist | Content-based filtering | Consistency, familiarity |

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): Did Min discuss how real systems handle mixed user types, or how user types can shift over time? -->
:::

## Classical Recommendation Paradigms

::: {.incremental}
- **Popularity-based:** Recommend globally popular items — no personalisation
- **Content-based filtering:** Recommend items similar to what the user has liked, based on item features
- **Collaborative filtering (CF):** Leverage patterns across many users — no item features needed
- **Hybrid approaches:** Combine multiple signals for robustness
:::

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): What specific examples or datasets did Min use to illustrate each paradigm? Were there any live demos? -->
:::

## The Cold-Start Problem

::: {.incremental}
- **New user cold-start:** No interaction history → cannot personalise
- **New item cold-start:** No ratings → cannot appear in CF recommendations
- **System cold-start:** Entirely new platform with no data
:::

**Strategies:**
- Use content features (bypasses interaction requirement)
- Ask users for explicit preferences onboarding
- Fall back to popularity-based recommendations

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): Were any specific industry solutions to cold-start discussed (e.g., onboarding surveys, zero-shot approaches)? -->
:::

## Ethics Thread: Popularity Bias and Exposure Inequality

- Popular items get recommended → more interactions → even more popular (**feedback loop**)
- Long-tail items receive little to no exposure
- Who bears the cost? **Niche creators, minority preferences, new entrants**

::: {.callout-warning}
Recommendation objectives that optimise purely for engagement can systematically disadvantage underrepresented content.
:::

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): What real-world examples did Min give? Were any papers on fairness in recommendation cited? -->

## Summary

| Method | Personalised? | Needs Item Features? | Cold-Start Robust? |
|--------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Popularity | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |
| Content-Based | ✓ | ✓ | Partial |
| User-Based CF | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Item-Based CF | ✓ | ✗ | Partial |
